title: Google Stitch
objectives: Understand Google Stitch via a real-life analogy
Use Stitch to generate UI mockups + prototypes from prompts
Export Stitch designs to Figma + code
Fit Stitch into a Flutter design workflow

sections.markdown:
**Think of Google Stitch as the AI intern that can produce a first-draft UI in 30 seconds.**

You describe a screen ('a settings page for a delivery app with dark mode, notification toggles, and a logout button'); Stitch generates a Figma-quality mockup, exports vector components, and lets you iterate via chat. Powered by Gemini + Google's design AI.

- **Prompt-to-UI** — natural language → clickable prototype.
- **Chat iteration** — 'make it more minimal,' 'switch to Material 3.'
- **Export** — Figma, HTML/CSS, code snippets.
- **Stitch Chats vs Canvases** — chat mode for iteration; canvas mode for precise editing.
- **Material Design 3 baseline** — output follows M3 conventions.
- **Multi-screen flows** — generate whole user journeys.

**Why Google Stitch matters for Flutter teams in 2026:** first-drafts of screens take minutes, not hours. Product managers can produce reviewable mockups without a designer. Designers accelerate from blank canvas → refined design. Engineers can start Flutter implementation from clean vectors + Material 3 tokens. **Limits:** AI output is generic; brand + micro-interactions still need human designers.

**Google Stitch** (announced 2024, generally available 2025+) is Google's AI-powered UI design tool. Uses Gemini to convert natural-language prompts + reference images into complete UI mockups, prototypes, and exportable code. Output follows Material Design 3 by default. Integrates with Figma export, HTML/CSS export, and future Android + iOS + Flutter code output. Web + upcoming native apps.

## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: Treating Stitch output as final.** AI first-drafts always need human polish — brand voice, micro-interactions, edge cases.
**Mistake 2: Skipping the prompt-refinement iteration.** First output is generic; specific prompts + chat iteration produce better results.
**Mistake 3: Ignoring accessibility.** Stitch output may not meet WCAG contrast + touch-target rules — audit.
**Mistake 4: Copying HTML/CSS output directly.** Web idioms don't map to Flutter widgets 1:1; use as reference, rewrite in Flutter.
**Mistake 5: No brand alignment.** Stitch defaults to generic Material 3; override with brand colors / typography.
**Mistake 6: Prompt overload.** Kitchen-sink prompt = mediocre output; iterate one concern at a time.
**Mistake 7: Skipping the Figma export.** Direct-to-code often lacks Figma-level refinability.
**Mistake 8: PII in reference images.** If uploading user screenshots, redact first.
## Best practices
**1. First-draft with Stitch; refine in Figma.**
**2. Iterative prompts** — one concern at a time.
**3. Reference images** for style anchoring.
**4. Brand palette + type from Variables** in Figma post-export.
**5. Accessibility audit** post-export.
**6. Use HTML/CSS as reference** only — implement in Flutter idioms.
**7. PM + designer + engineer** in the room during iteration.
**8. Sensitive data redacted** before uploading references.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — Generate a login screen from a text prompt.
**Practice 2 (Medium)** — Iterate a settings page 3 times with chat prompts.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — Export to Figma + apply brand tokens.
**Practice 4 (Hard)** — Multi-screen onboarding flow with prototype links.
**Practice 5 (Expert)** — Reference-image-driven design: upload competitor screenshot + prompt Stitch to design a similar-styled screen.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: When would you use Stitch vs Figma from scratch?**

**A:** **Stitch** for FIRST-DRAFTS + rapid iteration + when the design brief is 'we need something to react to.' Perfect for: PMs sketching a feature idea, engineers wireframing a screen for demo, designers accelerating early exploration. **Figma from scratch** for FINAL design + brand nuance + micro-interactions + design system work. Stitch's Material 3 baseline is generic; brand alignment + illustration + custom motion still need Figma craft. **Best workflow:** Stitch first-draft (15 min) → export to Figma → designer refines → tokens applied → Dev Mode hand-off. **Trap:** treating Stitch output as production-ready without human review + accessibility check + brand polish. Interviewer signal: knowing Stitch is a first-draft accelerator, not a designer replacement.

**Q2: How does Stitch fit into a Flutter team's workflow?**

**A:** **Pattern:** (1) **PM writes a feature spec** — 'add a settings page with X, Y, Z.' (2) **PM/designer uses Stitch** to generate a first mockup in 15 min. (3) **Design review** — 3 iterations via chat prompts. (4) **Export to Figma** — designer applies brand tokens + Auto Layout + variants. (5) **Dev Mode hand-off** to Flutter engineer. (6) **Flutter implementation** using theme tokens. **Speed win:** the traditional 'PM writes → designer produces → review → iterate' loop compresses from days to hours for early feedback. **Where Stitch doesn't help:** brand identity + complex flows + design-system-level decisions still need designer craft. **The Flutter angle:** Material 3 baseline maps well to Flutter's `MaterialApp` + `useMaterial3: true`; token export can drop into `ThemeData`. Interviewer signal: process integration, not just tool novelty.

**Q3: What are the accessibility risks of AI-generated UI?**

**A:** AI-generated designs often fail WCAG: (1) **Contrast** — low-contrast text/background (Stitch's generic palette may not meet AA/AAA). (2) **Touch targets** — buttons < 48×48 dp (Flutter's default requirement). (3) **Text scaling** — layouts break when user zooms. (4) **Screen reader labels** — icons without accessible names. (5) **Focus order** — non-linear tab order. (6) **Motion sensitivity** — flashy animations. **Mitigation:** post-generation audit with WCAG tools (axe, Contrast Checker), Flutter accessibility inspector, manual VoiceOver/TalkBack testing. **Regulator-aware:** EU + India accessibility laws increasingly apply to consumer apps. **AI won't solve accessibility for you** — treat as a first-draft that still requires human accessibility review. Interviewer signal: knowing AI doesn't absolve accessibility duty.

**Q4: How do prompt-engineering skills translate to Stitch?**

**A:** **Effective prompts include:** (1) **Screen type** — 'settings page,' 'onboarding step 2 of 4.' (2) **Design system baseline** — 'Material 3 dark mode.' (3) **Content specifics** — 'notification toggles: order updates, promotions.' (4) **Brand hints** — 'formal + trustworthy tone.' (5) **Layout constraints** — 'single-column mobile.' (6) **State** — 'error state.' (7) **Reference** — 'similar to Google Maps settings.' **Iterative refinement:** 'Move the profile row to the top' > 'Fix the layout.' **Anti-patterns:** vague ('modern + cool'); kitchen-sink (10 requirements at once); no context (no target device). **Same rules apply as LLM prompting:** specific, iterative, well-scoped. **Interviewer signal:** knowing prompt engineering IS design skill in AI tools.

**Q5: How would you evaluate whether Stitch output is production-ready?**

**A:** **Checklist:** (1) **Brand alignment** — colors, typography, tone match brand. (2) **Accessibility** — WCAG AA contrast, touch targets, focus order, screen reader labels. (3) **Design system consistency** — reuses existing components, doesn't invent new ones. (4) **Content clarity** — copy is clear + not placeholder. (5) **Edge cases** — empty states, error states, loading states shown. (6) **Multi-form-factor** — mobile + tablet + landscape considered. (7) **Interaction states** — hover, pressed, disabled variants. (8) **Motion** — respects prefers-reduced-motion. (9) **Localization** — text expansion + RTL considered. (10) **Legal / compliance** — regulator-required disclosures included. **First-draft rarely passes all 10;** designer refinement + engineer review closes gaps.

**Q6: What are the ethical + IP considerations?**

**A:** **(1) Training data provenance** — Stitch trained on public + licensed designs; output may echo styles of specific brands. Avoid outputs that clone competitor UI. **(2) Attribution + license** — Google's Stitch terms; generally you own outputs but check current TOS. **(3) Brand safety** — don't upload internal designs to public tools without approval. **(4) Reference-image copyright** — uploading a screenshot may create derivative-work claims. **(5) Employee handoff** — as team member, ensure AI-tool use aligns with employer policy. **(6) Client work** — client contracts may forbid AI-generated deliverables. **(7) Disclosure** — some regulators (EU AI Act) may require disclosing AI-generated design in certain contexts. **(8) Sustainability** — AI compute has energy cost; batch usage is more efficient. **Interviewer signal:** professional maturity + not naive on AI ethics.

## Real-world usage

- **PM sketching** — feature ideas without a designer.
- **Designer acceleration** — first-drafts in minutes.
- **Engineer wireframes** — visual comm before code.
- **Design system exploration** — variant discovery.
- **NOT for** — finalized designs; brand identity; complex flows without human refinement.

## Advanced notes

- **Multi-modal input** — text + reference images.
- **Chat mode vs Canvas mode** — iteration vs precision.
- **Figma export** — with variables + Auto Layout preserved.
- **HTML/CSS export** — reference-quality; not production Flutter.
- **Multi-screen flows** — Stitch links + adds prototype transitions.
- **Material 3 default** — override via prompt for other systems.
- **Version history** — chat log preserves iteration.
- **Team collaboration** — share Stitch canvases with team.
- **AI + design system** — Stitch respects brand tokens if provided.
- **Trade-offs vs Codemagic AI** — Stitch focuses on design; Codemagic AI on full app scaffolding.
- **Vertex AI Design Studio** — Google's related enterprise offering.
- **Alternatives** — v0 by Vercel, Uizard, Galileo AI, Framer AI.
- **Trend** — AI + designer + engineer collaboration; not designer replacement.
